title_original: Paris Photo 2026 : My Feeling by Thierry Maindrault
excerpt_original: The great financial high mass of Photography has gathered once again in Paris, as every year in mid-autumn, with its officiants (specialist galleries) and […] Cet article Paris Photo 2026 : My Feeling by Thierry Maindrault est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography…

blocks.text: The great financial high mass of Photography has gathered once again in Paris, as every year in mid-autumn, with its officiants (specialist galleries) and its flock (collectors and other buyers, public ones included). In recent years, this little world, once as respectable as it was respected, has seen the curious arrive (whether or not they love images), impatient to declare, urbi et orbi, that they were indeed present. And so a serious show where photographers, gallerists, collectors and public authorities rubbed shoulders to redefine the creative and economic situation of authors has become a fair. I have always found it strange, financial calculations of the organizers aside (the show was not free, and neither is the fair), this new mixture, which has no justifiable purpose. Photography having (in spite of itself) invaded, quantitatively, almost every possible space, the justification of a new visibility has become obsolete. This questioning, by way of preamble, is in no way a criticism or a reproach, just an intellectual question about the mixing of genres that is taking hold of our societies. My baker sells cold cuts and my talented florist delivers parcels from China! The scope of action defines the fields of competence, and highly specialized training rarely produces multi-operational individuals.

That being established, the principle of an open market, professionally and so well steered by its director, as it currently is in Paris, remains indispensable. All those around Photography, in particular authors and their representatives, can only rejoice in this event.

In the general interest, a few indiscretions picked up along the way, which are so much easier coming from a third party. Especially if your position obliges you to pay compliments, for fear of reprisals.

On the gallerists’ side: those who pay for and fit out a booth to present the works of their “protégés.” Being at Paris Photo is always prestigious; but it is becoming very expensive relative to sales, which no longer always cover the investment. A single professional day (even extended) is not enough before the wild hordes come in. The invasion of the booths, with no real economic return over four days, becomes very heavy in time, fatigue and security. Paris Photo has become a fair, with no potential buyers in view of what the galleries offer. It must not become a festival; there are already too many of those. The socially hot period in Paris has deterred a number of foreign investors from making the trip to Paris.

On the collectors’ side: those people who reach into their wallets to acquire a work, to speculate or sometimes out of personal taste. They are always delighted to find a unique, hushed environment in which they can catch a glimpse of what is new, what is available and above all what can (for a great many of them) turn a profit. Paris Photo is always easier than running from a gallery to a studio, from an exhibition to a festival. The danger is that Paris Photo has spawned imitators, and many large American and European cities have promoted their own events. I won’t even mention the Asian region, which, as in every field, is making up for lost time to take the lead. On top of that comes the matter of Paris Photo’s reason for being, with those “aristocrats” of the photographic image vanishing as the steamrollers of patronage arrive. These are the powerful Foundations, with their nearly inexhaustible – semi-public – finances. The photographic object of acquisition definitively loses its status as a “favorite” to become a tenant of vaults and generate a little buzz through highly publicized loans.

On the general public’s side: the crowds that press in, from cradle to coffin, to prove they passed through the aisles of the Grand Palais. The flow of visitors (which is now used to measure the power of an event) sometimes trickles with difficulty through aisles that cut across and crisscross one another. For roughly three or four years now, elegance has strolled the aisles alongside an unbridled vulgarity. Strollers perform gymkhanas, at times acrobatic, between calves. Now and then, some tell a personal anecdote, glued (almost permanently) in front of a photograph. Some will leave with all the exhibited photos in their smartphone. Note that freedom of expression still bursts forth in front of a partition lined with a booth, which is always a good sign in an era when silence is truly becoming the gospel. The public is on the whole satisfied: it paid dearly to be part of the photography world, and it was able to lay its hands on images in the back rooms of the booths (a form of initiation). It regrets not having been able to see the prices of the works, which are no longer displayed at almost any booth. It is also frustrated by how few exhibitors speak French. Finally, it leaves smiling, its hybrid camera paired with a very big “rock” or the latest-model Leica on its belly.
So there you are, caught up in the atmosphere, my dear friends, you who could not, or do not wish to, come and spend your gold écus on three or four Parisian days.
How about talking a little about photographs!

The trend of the past three years is intensifying. The market, which is becoming financial (as set out above), does not want to take too many risks. This brings a very high proportion of vintage prints, preferred over recent creative work. Investors are paying for safe havens. It is a pity that some naïve buyers do not realize that in the heaps of prints pulled from attic trunks, not everything is viable, technically or artistically. As long as there are suckers, I do not see why certain galleries (supposedly competent) would do the sorting.

It should also be noted that vintage (often fake, incidentally) has grown younger since this year, with the notable arrival of photographs from the end of the last century. An amusing observation: most of the images on offer are reportage, generally with little or no creativity or originality. It does not matter, since financial speculation is now done on authors’ names and no longer on photographic images.
The so-called emerging photography section is as dismal as ever; many of the presentations risk ending up submerged unless a powerful Foundation throws them a lifebuoy.
Given the mass of photographs on show, it must be admitted that there are a few gems in the galleries that do the job. You just have to find them, which is not quite normal at such an event.

We are all waiting for the 2027 edition, hoping for a reinvented show, once again at the forefront of worldwide proposals, rather than lagging behind the ideas and fashions of the moment. For two hundred years, photography has been at the cutting edge of technology and human creation. Today, authors and photographic creators are suffering; yet they are still able to trust the management team and its brilliant director, Florence Bourgeois, to lead human intelligence toward new dreams.
